text:
Verses 172-174

(7:172) When your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and He made them bear witness over themselves, [He said to them,] “Am I not your Lord?” They said, “Yes indeed! We bear witness.” [This,] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, “Indeed we were unaware of this,”

(7:173) or lest you should say, “Our fathers ascribed partners [to Allah] before [us] and we were descendants after them. Will You then destroy us because of what the falsifiers have done?”

(7:174) Thus do We elaborate the communications, and so that they may come back.

Introduction

These verses refer to God’s covenant with the Children of Adam concerning His Lordship. They are among the most subtle verses of the Qur’an

in terms of meaning, and the most elegant in terms of expression.

Commentary

(7:172) When your Lord took (akhadhnā, from akhdh) from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and He made them bear witness over themselves, [He said to them,] “Am I not your Lord?” They said, “Yes indeed! We bear witness.” [This,] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, “Indeed we were unaware of this.”

When something is “taken” (akhdh) from something else, it means that it is separated from it as an independent entity in one way or another. This can vary according to context and usage. Some examples are: (1) Taking a bite from a food, or taking a sip of water from a glass. (2) Taking money or possessions from a robber, a generous person, a seller, or a lender. (3) Taking knowledge from a scholar, taking [intellectual] provision from a session, taking pleasure from meeting a friend. (4) Taking a child from the father for education.

These applications show that the mere usage of the verb akhdh does not clarify the meaning unless more is added. That is why God complements it with: from the Children of Adam. This shows that they were

separated and differentiated from one another.

… from their loins…: The partitive particle “from” (min) shows that only a part of the original object was taken, such that it maintained its form and did not lose its completeness and independence. The piece that was taken was then completed to become an independent object of the same kind. The child is initially a part of the parents, but then it is taken from their loins, separated as a new entity, and developed into a complete human being. Subsequently, another child is taken from the loin of this person, until every person is extracted and all parts are separated from their initial wholes. Then all humans become distinct, and stand as independent individuals. Each has their own soul, and will bear the good or

evil consequences of their own deeds. This is what we can deduce from the expression: When your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants. Had the verse not mentioned from their loins, or had it said, “When your Lord dispersed the Children of Adam,” the meaning would have remained ambiguous.

… and He made them bear witness (ashhadahum) over themselves…:

This sentence refers to another divine act with the Children of Adam after completely separating them from one another. To make one bear witness over something means summoning the witness to the scene and showing them the fact of the matter so that they may observe it directly. Making them witness over themselves means showing the reality of themselves to them in a way that they observe what He wants them to observe about themselves, so that they can later testify to what they witnessed whenever they are questioned about it [in God’s court of justice on the Day of

Judgment].

Every soul has some relations with other things, and one could be made witness over any of them. This is clarified by: “Am I not your Lord?” That is what they were made to witness. God’s purpose was that they may witness His Lordship, so that they would testify to it whenever questioned about it.

No matter how proud and arrogant one becomes; no matter to what extent one is supported by favorable circumstances; no matter how much one is deceived by the availability of all means and facilities; still no one can deny in themselves that they do not own themselves and are not independent in managing their affairs. If one were their own owner, they would

have shielded themselves against misfortunes like death, pain, and disaster. And if one were independent in managing their affairs, they would

not need to resort to different means and instruments in the world, even though one may view oneself as having full control and dominance over those instruments. Moreover, one would realize that their means, instruments and connections are equally in need of what lies beyond them. They

are subservient to a higher Ruler, whether He rules for or against them. It is not up to one to remove one’s needs and fulfill one’s wishes.

The need for God—that is, our Owner and Director—is the reality of the human being. Poverty is inscribed on our souls; weakness is sealed on our foreheads. This is not concealed from anyone with the slightest degree of reason, whether they are educated or illiterate, old or young, noble or lay. This means that the human beings, in any stage of their human existence, witness in themselves that they have a Lord Who owns them and

directs their affairs. How could they not witness their Lord when they witness their essential need? Is it conceivable that one may realize a need in oneself without realizing the other side to whom one is in need?1 … “Am I not your Lord?”…: This is what God made them witness.

… They said, “Yes indeed! We bear witness”…: This shows that they witnessed the above reality and acknowledged it.

1 When we see anything, what we see is light. Realizing the inherent darkness of anything is tantamount to realizing the light which makes it visible. (Trans.) Our explanations above should clarify what some exegetes have said: The verse refers to what humans observe throughout their life in this world. They see in themselves that they are needy with respect to every aspect of their existence and every law and property that revolves around it. Therefore, the meaning of the verse is: We created the Children of Adam in the earth, and We differentiated them through birth and procreation. We made them aware of their need and subjugation to Us, and they admitted that, saying: “Yes indeed! We bear witness that You are our Lord.”

Based on the above, there are two possible interpretations for: “Yes indeed! We bear witness.” (1) It is an expression of their condition and state (called lisān al-ḥāl), not something that they literally said. (2) It is a necessary implication of something that they said: They acknowledged that they

are needy, and that necessarily implies acknowledging the One Whom they need. The difference between the two is that in the first case, the meaning is deduced from a quality or condition of the person or a thing, even

if the that person or thing is unaware of it. For instance, the remnants of a ruined city “speak” of what happened to its people: “The life of this world turned them into its plaything, until they were trampled upon by the galloping of time; thus their peal dropped and their breaths stopped.” Another example is how the appearance of a poor person “speaks” of their poverty, need and adversity. In the second case, however, the meaning is deduced from what one says, as its entailment or corollary. Either of these two kinds of speech can interpret the acknowledgment mentioned in the verse: They said, “Yes indeed! We bear witness.” The first interpretation— that they confessed through lisān al-ḥāl (language of condition or state)— is more plausible because the verse is about testimony, which requires a direct and clear statement, not an implication of another statement.1 It should be clarified that their witnessing of the scene [implied by “Yes indeed! We bear witness”] occurred in the same sense and way that God showed them the scene, implied by: He made them bear witness over themselves. He took their acknowledgment through the same “tongue” that He

spoke to them. Based on this, we can offer a third way of communication to interpret this witnessing. This is based on the application of “speech”

1 Lisān al-ḥāl is what is understood from a person’s condition and mode of being. Its opposite is lisān al-qāl (language of words), which is when someone actively expresses something, either through sound waves or otherwise. (Trans.)

to God. God’s speech is any divine act that reveals God’s objectives and intentions. As we have repeatedly discussed, a real [and not metaphorical] sense of God’s speech is His act of ījād (existentiation, giving existence to something). The connection between the two may not be self-evident at first, but it will become clear with some analysis. Therefore, the question and answer here—“Am I not your Lord?”and “Yes indeed! We bear

witness”—can be interpreted in the light of this mode of communication [through one’s purposeful action]. We shall discuss this further below. Either way, this verse—When your Lord took from the Children of Adam…—describes three events: (1) God separated the Children of Adam from one another. (2) He made each of them witness over their self. (3) He took their acknowledgment of His Lordship. The purpose of this witnessing and acknowledgment is then described in the last part of the verse and the following verse: [This,] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, “Indeed we were unaware of this,” or lest you should say, “Our fathers ascribed partners [to Allah] before [us] and we were descendants after them. Will You then destroy us because of what the falsifiers have done?”

(7:172-173). People could dispute with God on the Day of Resurrection based on either of these two arguments, had it not been for the above witnessing and acknowledgment of His Lordship. The verse’s context shows that now they are lefiiwith no argument for associating partners with Him, while He will be fully justified in dooming the violators to hell. The word “or” (the Arabic particle aw) at the beginning of verse 7:173 shows a parallel between the two arguments in these verses. Both are based on the knowledge that results from the above mentioned witnessing, and both are narrated from the Children of Adam who were separated from one another. Upon further reflection on these verses, we can see that these two arguments pertain to two possible alternatives to the above act of witnessing. The two arguments can be elaborated as follows:

(1) [This,] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, “Indeed we were unaware of this” (7:172). This could be the people’s argument against Us had We not taken their testimony at all. We took the descendants of the Children of Adam from their loins and made them bear witness over themselves. They acknowledged Our Lordship, and that completed Our proof against them on the Day of Resurrection. Had We not done this at all—that is, had We not made each of them to witness their self and testify that God is their Lord—all of them would have argued against Us on the Day of Resurrection. They would say that they were unaware of Our Lordship in this life, and unaware individuals are exempt from obligation and rebuke.

(2) Or lest you should say, “Our fathers ascribed partners [to Allah] before [us] and we were descendants after them. Will You then destroy us because of what the falsifiers have done?” (7:173). This could be people’s argument against Us had We not taken their testimony partially.

That would be the case if only some of them were made witness over themselves, but not others—meaning that only the fathers witnessed this momentous reality, but not their children.1 In that case, if they associated partners with God, the polytheism of the fathers would be despite their knowledge that their Lord is God alone, and no one else. That would be a sin on their part. Meanwhile, the polytheism of the children would be out of mere conformity in a matter that they had no way of knowing it, whether in detail or in brief. While the fathers would be sinful in associating partners with God—because of their knowledge of the truth—the

children simply followed their fathers in their practice. It was the fathers who led their children on the way of polytheism through how they raised and educated them. The children had no way to learn the fact of the matter. How could they know that their fathers erred themselves, and also

led them into error? So the descendants could argue against God on the Day of Resurrection, saying that it was the fathers who sinfully associated partners with God and violated the truth. That was an act of the fathers, and they alone should be taken to task. When someone does not know a truth to begin with, they cannot be charged with the duty to observe it, which in turn makes their disobedience meaningless. Hence, the children did not disobey or violate this truth. This means that God would not have a complete argument against the descendants, which would make His argument against the whole humankind incomplete.

Question: This is not a complete picture because the two arguments [at the end of verse 7:172 and in verse 7:173] do not cover all the possible arguments that humankind could present against God. There are two other possibilities that are not covered here: (a) W hat if only the children were made witness over themselves, but not the fathers? (b) What if only some

1 “Fathers” and “children refer to the early and later generations of humankind, respectively. (Trans.)

of the descendants were made witness over themselves [but not all the descendants, and not their ancestors]? This is confirmed by the evolution of human knowledge and civilization, where the subsequent generations inherit what their predecessors have lef , and add more to that. Hence, the later generations achieve what the former ones lacked.

Answer: These two cases would also fall under the arguments expressed in these verses. God’s argument would still be complete against either all descendants of humankind, or against those of them who witnessed the truth. If some of the ancestors [that is, the early generations]

did not witness the truth, it means that they were completely heedless of God’s Lordship, so they could not be held responsible for their polytheism. Hence, they could argue by the first statement: “Indeed we were unaware of this” (7:172). The second argument is not applicable to them because they were not preceded by others to follow them.

The evolution of human knowledge and civilization pertains to acquired knowledge that humans learn through experience gradually. That is different from one’s knowledge of oneself and one’s need of a Lord Who manages one’s affairs. That kind of knowledge is not empirical, but is present with everyone inherently. It is among our intrinsic cognitions, which are the roots of all other branches of human knowledge. It does not make sense for these types of knowledge to develop after what depends on them. As it has been proven in its place, the gradual development of human knowledge is a result of their inner sense of need [to develop various disciplines].

In short, the two verses are saying that God differentiated between the Children of Adam by taking some of them out of others, and then made them witness over themselves and took their covenant concerning His Lordship. As a result, none of them is unaware of that testimony

and their covenant. Hence, neither can they all argue against God on the account of being heedless of it, nor can some of them claim exemption on the account of their fathers having led them into polytheism.

The View of the Opponents of the World of Pre-Existence Based on the above summary, some exegetes have said that “when” in this verse—When your Lord took—refers to our life in this world (dunyā). These two verses [7:172-173] describe God’s ongoing process of creating humans in this world: He first transfers the seeds of humans from the loins of their fathers to the wombs of their mothers, and then from there to this world. Then, during their life, He makes them witness over themselves, and shows them the signs of His creation and unity. They witness

how they are in need from head to toe, which proves His existence and oneness. This is equivalent to asking them: “Am I not your Lord?” To this question, they answer through their mode of being (lisān al-ḥāl): “Yes indeed! We bear witness.” They effectively admit that “Thou art our Lord, and we have no other lord but Thee!” God does this so that people may not argue with Him on the Day of Resurrection. This way, they cannot claim that they were unaware and did not know Him; or that it was their fathers who associated partners with Him, but the children had no clue about it since they were raised in an environment of shirk (association, polytheism) without being responsible for it.

The above mentioned exegetes have rejected a number of narrations which talk about the world of pre-existence (ʿālam al-dharr). According to these narrations, there was a realm prior to this world, where God brought out all descendants of Adam from his loin in the form of small atoms (or ants), made them witness themselves, introduced Himself to them, and made a covenant with them concerning His Lordship. That is a decisive proof against them on the Day of Resurrection. The exegetes have rejected these narrations for contravening the apparent meaning of the Qur’an. Their reasons for this are the following:

(1) Were the descendants of Adam who were taken out of his loin intelligent or not? If they were not intelligent beings, then they could not recognize God’s unity and be addressed by Him. If they were intelligent beings who are held accountable for a pledge that they gave, then they must remember that scene. A covenant is a decisive proof only when the person remembers it, as the verse explicitly says: [This,] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, “Indeed we were unaware of this” (7:172). However, we do not remember any prior creation to our existence here in this world. Hence, what is meant in the verse can only pertain to what we comprehend in this world, and that is the need we find in ourselves to a Lord Who owns us and manages our affairs. That is the Lord of all things. (2) It is not possible for a large number of rational beings to forget something, to the extent that not even a single one of them remembers it. The lapse between this life and the claimed world of pre-existence is not longer than the lapse between this world and the next, where the inhabitants of paradise and hell will remember what they went through in this world, as we can see in several verses such as: One of them will say, “Indeed I had a companion…” (37:51); And they say, “What is the matter with us that we do not see [here] men whom we used to count among the bad ones?” (38:62).

Besides, if it is possible for such a large number of individuals to forget, then it is also possible that our current life is a reincarnation following a previous round of existence where we were charged with certain

obligations to follow. We do not remember this, but we are going through the consequences of our actions in our previous life [that is, our karma]. This is the same as the theory of transmigration (tanāsukh), which interprets the hereafter as the passing of the soul from one body to another

through rebirth.1

(3) The narrations talk about the loin of Adam, but the verse talks about the loin of the Children of Adam. The verse says their loins and their descendants [in plural], not “his loin” and “his descendants.” Therefore, the verse apparently does not include Adam’s immediate progeny. Moreover, the verses say that God did this so that they may not say on the Day of Resurrection, “Indeed we were unaware of this,” or that “Our fathers ascribed partners [to Allah] before [us] and we were descendants after them…” (7:172- 173). These statements show that the descendants in this verse had fathers who were polytheists.

Based on this, some scholars have said that these verses include only some of Adam’s descendants, not all of them. They exclude Adam, his immediate children, all believers, and those polytheists whose fathers were not polytheists. Therefore, the verses only apply to those polytheists who were born to polytheist parents.

(4) The world of pre-existence was presumably a realm where all humankind was gathered together as a single whole. This contradicts the idea that “Our fathers ascribed partners [to Allah]”(7:173), which shows that they had polytheist fathers.

(5) Some exegetes have accepted these narrations as authentic, but not as an interpretation of the verse. Instead these narrations pertain to how God fashioned humankind before their appearance in this world:

1 This point is raised as an objection because reincarnation is against the apparent Qur’anic view of afterlife. (Trans.)

He hard-wired them to know His Lordship. Hence, these narrations fall in the same category as narrations which say that “All humans are born with a divine intuition and a monotheistic nature (fiṭrah).” Similarly, it is said that children [who die before puberty] will be in a blissful state in paradise because of their belief in God in the world of pre-existence. Meanwhile, the verse has nothing to do with the message of these narrations. The central theme of the verse is that God did this so that the people would not argue with Him on the Day of Resurrection, saying that they were unaware of this. If the verse were about what He did

to them in the world of pre-existence, then they would still have a case against God. They could argue: “Our Lord, it is true that You showed us ourselves when You took us out of Adam’s loin, and that we were certain about Your Lordship just as we are today—on the Day of Resurrection— but You made us forget that scene during our life in the world, which was the place of religious obligation and action. You lefiius to our own intellects to discover Your Lordship independently. Thus, those of us who could prove Your Lordship intellectually accepted it; and those of us who could not, did not. Both groups followed the rule of their reason. So what is our sin in all this? You took away from us the memory of that witnessing, and instead equipped us with a faculty whose job is to reason, which

may either hit or miss.”

(6) There is no clear connection between the verse and what is found in the narrations because the scene depicted in the verse could be a symbolic illustration. The narrations [which imply a literal occurrence of such

a testimony in a previous world] are not authoritative because their chain of transmission is either unconnected (called marfūʿ) or they end with the Prophet’s Companions (called mawqūf).

The above list was a summary of the arguments of some scholars concerning the purport of the verse and the validity of the narrations. The Response of the Proponents

The proponents of the world of pre-existence (ʿālam al-dharr)—which include the majority of the scholars of hadith, and some exegetes—have given some responses to these arguments. Here is a summary of their answers to the above points:

(1) The fact that humans have forgotten the scene and its details does not harm the validity of God’s proof against them. What is problematic is if the covenant is entirely lost, which means that people forget God’s oneness as their Lord. This, however, is not forgotten and is never effaced from

their souls. That suffices for a binding contract. For instance, suppose you want to make an agreement with Zayd, so you invite him to your house, treat him with honor, and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the situation with him as much as you can. You go through all the details together, and he signs the agreement with you. Then he is responsible for his agreement as long as he remembers its overall occurrence, even though he may forget coming to your house and all the details that transpired between you at that time.

(2) There is no logical impossibility for a large number of rational beings to forget something. Rather, it is only a matter of unlikelihood [which does not equate impossibility]. Moreover, as stated in the previous answer, the basic knowledge of God’s Lordship is not forgotten, and

that is sufficient for humankind’s responsibility. Also, if one admits that people may have forgotten what occurred to them prior to this life, it does not prove the theory of tanāsukh (transmigration, reincarnation). There are other problems that disprove that theory, which have been discussed in its place. Overall, there is no proof for claiming that it is impossible for people to forget the events of one realm when they move to another. (3) The verse also includes the immediate progeny of Adam. The verse’s expression—When your Lord took from the Children of Adam—is sufficient to show this, because it clearly means that first Adam’s immediate children were taken out of his loin, and then their children were in turn taken out of their loins, and so on until the last descendants. This is just like the sequence of generations in this world, which occurs through procreation and birth. Al-Rāzī has responded to this differently: the narrations talk about the extraction of Adam’s immediate children from his loin, and the verse talks about the extraction of their children from their loins. Hence, the verse and the narrations build on each other and complete the picture.1 The narrations which talk about Adam’s immediate children—that God took them out of Adam’s loin and made a covenant with them—do not intend to interpret the text of the verse, but they serve to elaborate on the story. Therefore, one cannot refute them on the account of being inconsistent with the Qur’an or contradictory to it.

1 The problem with al-Rāzī’s explanation should be clear. (Auth.)

There is also a problem with scholars who have limited the verse’s application to those individuals whose fathers were polytheists. They have excluded Adam’s immediate children, and anyone whose father was not a polytheist, from the verse’s scope. This is based on the assumption that the verse is only meant as an argument against the polytheists,

intended to strip them of the claim that “Our fathers ascribed partners [to Allah].” They have concluded this restriction of application because only the polytheists would make this argument, not all individuals. However, these scholars have missed the purpose of the verse, because the claim is ascribed to all people as a general and overall statement, not as a claim that every one of them would make individually. The meaning is: Had We not done so, then all of you could argue, if they were to be punished on the Day of Resurrection: “I did not associate partners, but those who were before me did so, and I was only a descendant and follower of them, not a leader myself.”

(4) The answer to the fourth problem should be clear based on the above. The verse and the narrations imply that God separated the parents and their children in that realm of pre-existence, then He returned them again to the state of being together as a single whole.

(5) This is against the apparent purport of some narrations, and against the explicit text of others. As for the problem of forgetting the covenant, it was answered under number (1).

(6) The apparent sense (ẓāhir) of a statement is authoritative; it does not have to be direct or explicit (taṣrīḥ). Just because one can interpret something symbolically does not prove that it should be interpreted as such. We can opt for a symbolic meaning only if there is an obstacle to interpreting the text based on its apparent meaning. In this case, we explained that there is no such obstacle.

As for the claim that these narrations are weak and unreliable: that is not true. Among them there are also authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) and reliable (muwaththaq) narrations in terms of transmission.1 The above was a summary of the debate over the world of pre-existence in the light of this verse, including the views of those who accept

and defend it, and those who reject and doubt it. However, upon adequate

1 We shall present these in our examination of narrations below, by God’s will. (Auth.)

contemplation on the verse and the narrations, and on the arguments of the proponents and opponents, we are led in a different direction than what the two groups have disagreed upon.

Examining the View of the Proponents

In short, here is the view of those who have accepted the narrations about the world of pre-existence, and have used them to interpret the verse:

When God created Adam in the form of a complete man, He extracted his seed from his loin—the seed that later turned into his progeny. Ho took that out of him, and then again extracted parts of that seed which would later become its children. He separated the essential parts of each seed from the parts that would later grow into its children. Thus He continued sequentially until the very last part that would become another

human being. In other words, God took out Adam’s seed—which was the main material for humankind—and then divided it consecutively and indefinitely, such that every human being was separated and distinguished from that seed. That resulted in a countless number of dispersed particles. At that point—or before that—God made each particle into a complete human: exactly the same as the person that the initial particle would grow to be in this world. The part that would later become Zayd, was the very Zayd there; and the part that would later become ʿAmr, was the very ʿAmr there. God gave them life and consciousness, and equipped them with the means of hearing and speech. He enabled them to understand meanings, and to choose to either disclose or conceal them. Then He introduced Himself to them. He spoke to them and they responded positively. They all acknowledged His Lordship, some of them in accordance to what they genuinely held in their hearts, and some of them contrary to that. After making this covenant with them, God returned them to their original position in the loins recursively, until they were all gathered again in Adam’s loin, while still retaining their knowledge of God’s Lordship, even though they may have forgotten the scene of the witnessing and the making of the covenant. These individuals are really existent in the loins of their fathers until they are permitted to enter the world. They come to this world carrying with themselves their initial knowledge of God’s Lordship. That is their own verdict that they have a Lord based on observing in themselves a need for Someone Who owns them and directs their affairs. This is what the proponents of the world of pre-existence have understood from the narrations and the verse, and that is what they wish to

prove. However, this is logically impossible, and is also rejected by the Qur’an and hadith without a doubt. How could they prove that a single part of Zayd—which is one of his particles that was transmitted from Adam’s loin to his son, and from his loin to his son, and so on consecutively until it reached Zayd—is the same as Zayd himself? How could that particle be proven to have cognition, consciousness, hearing, sight and heart?

How could that particle be charged with religious obligations, covenants and commitments? How could it be held accountable for God’s arguments that are addressed to it? How could Zayd be rewarded or penalized based on that particle’s covenant? Based on both rational proof and scriptural evidence, the reality of a human being is something beyond the person’s material substance. It is one’s soul which is created with the creation of one’s body in this world. We had some discussion on this topic before.1 Moreover, it is proven [in logic] that all statements (taṣdīqāt) hinge upon a set of concepts (taṣawwurāt). This includes both statements that are self-evident (badīhiyyāt) and the ones that are derived (naẓariyyāt), including the admittance that one has a Lord Who owns them and directs their affairs. The concepts are themselves acquired through inner and outer sensations, which both hinge on having a compound material being. This is the case of all acquired knowledge of humans, one of which is the statement that there is a Lord Who takes care of one’s needs.

The verse is clearly saying that the witnessing and the covenant were meant to complete God’s argument against humankind. Now, there are two conditions that come into play here: (1) The other side must be intelligent. (2) The other side must recognize their Lord [through feeling a

need in themselves]. If both conditions are required for the completeness of God’s argument, then the above notion of the world of pre-existence suffers from the fact that the particles lose their intellect once they return to their original position in the loins, until they appear again in this world. Even if they retain their intellect all the way through the loins and wombs, they must lose it upon their birth, and lack it until they reach the age of reason. This undermines God’s argument against humankind. And if we

1 See volume 2 (1st ed.), pp. 201ffof the English translation, under verses 2:153-

157. (Trans.)

claim that only the second condition—of knowledge of the Lord—is sufficient for the completeness of God’s argument, then there would be no

need for a world of pre-existence, because that condition can be met by the view of those who have rejected these narrations.1 Alternatively, we can imagine three possibilities here:

(1) God’s argument hinges on all of what happened in that realm— including the witnessing, the recognition, and the covenant.

Comment: The problem with this view is that then God’s argument would fall short with the forgetting of any of these. We have forgotten the scene of our witnessing, God’s speech with us, and the making of the covenant.

(2) If God’s argument hinges only on the knowledge of His Lordship. The other events—the witnessing and the covenant—were rather meant to establish this knowledge. But once the knowledge is there, God’s argument does not depend on them anymore.

Comment: The problem with this view is that it means that everyone is accountable to God’s argument and covenant, including fetuses, infants, the mentally retarded, and the ignorant. This is against both rational and scriptural evidence.

(3) The knowledge of God’s Lordship becomes complete and binding only once one matures and develops rationally. This occurred in the world of pre-existence, whereby God’s argument became complete against the individuals. Then the conditions of maturity and reason receded, leaving the knowledge as an insufficient proof. Then, whoever matures and

develops rationally in this world, God’s argument is made complete against them for a second time.

Comment: The problem with this view is that just as one develops rationally in this world through certain means and instruments, one’s knowledge of God’s Lordship can also develop through worldly channels and experiences. One’s rational faculty—that is, one’s power of distinction between good and bad—grows through the repeated occurrence of various events, and through consistent practice and experience in life. This is

a gradual process and continuum with perfection of the intellect at one end, and its utter weakness at the other. A similar paradigm can be held to

Now we shall examine the view of the opponents of the world of preexistence. They claim that the verse describes the current state of human

Since He makes them realize how they are immersed in need and weakness, it is as though He is asking them, “Am I not your Lord?” And as they hear this question, they admit: “Yes indeed! God does this in order to complete His proof and to cut offtheir argument against Him, because now they know. This way they cannot bring the excuse that they were unaware of this. The word idh indicates the temporal container of an event, and is especially used for past events. Sometimes it is also used for future events that are certain. We are the audience of these verses in our current state of existence. Our View

When your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants: We can deduce two points from this expression: (1) On the one hand, it matches what we observe in this world. The verse talks about God’s creation of humankind, where each person issues from another, and a small number [of early ancestors] proliferates into a multitude. This is how the individuals come to existence successively, and also

how the species is maintained through the continuation of its members. (2) Nevertheless, this expression also indicates some sense of precedence. It implies something “prior” to our current course of creation that is readily observable to us.

This precedence cannot be temporal, as we discussed above. Temporal precedence to this world means that God took out from the first human being his seed which would later evolve into all humanity, differentiated it into as many particles as the number of individuals who would come to existence, and then gave every one of them the exact same properties of life, intellect, hearing, sight, heart, back and stomach. All these developments occurred before their natural course. Then He showed Himself to

them and took their covenant, and then He returned them to their positions in the loins so that they may complete their natural course there until

they come to life in this world. As we explained, this is impossible, and the verse does not support this notion. The reason why this is impossible is that it necessitates every person to exist twice in this world. It entails a worldly existence and personality prior to another worldly existence and personality for every individual.1 This means that every person would at the same time be themselfiand other than themself. He also affirms another life for humans in the world of barzakh (the intermediate realm between this life and the Resurrection), which is governed by different laws and properties than this world, although the individuals there will be the same as the individuals in this world. Furthermore, God says: There is not a thing but that its stores are with Us, and We do not send it down except in a known measure (15:21). This verse says that everything has another existence in the stores of God; an existence which is vast and not yet measured out. It becomes determined and delimited when God sends it to this world. For instance, the human world, notwithstanding its vastness, has another existence with God in His stores, which takes precedence to its existence in this world. W hat exists here is a result of that higher and prior existence descending to this world. The existence of all beings in this world—including humankind—is gradual and subject to time and change. Yet, this gradual existence is itself granted by God immediately and instantaneously, through the divine command, “Be!” (kun). This notion is found in several verses, such as: All His command, when He wills something, is to say to it “Be,” and it is. So glory be to Him in Whose hand is the kingdom of all things (36:82-83); And Our command is but a single [word], like the twinkling of an eye (54:50). This means that this world and all things in it have two aspects: (1) They have a worldly aspect by which they face the world. This aspect of their existence is governed by time and change: they progress gradually from potentiality to actuality, and from non-being to being. They grow from imperfection step by step until they reach their perfection, then they die and return to their Lord. (2) They have a divine aspect by which they face God. This is a non-temporal and non-gradual existence that they have. Their divine aspect possesses all its properties timelessly, without going through the stages of perfection from potentiality to actualization. This aspect is different from the first one, although they are two sides of the same coin. The two aspects are not governed by the same laws. It requires fine intellectual ability to imagine and comprehend this second aspect of all things. We had some discussion on it previously, and we shall elaborate on it more below, by God’s will.1

These verses [concerning the divine aspect of things] indicate that the human world, notwithstanding its vastness and extension, has an assembled and concentrated existence with God. This is the aspect by which humanity faces God, and through which God bestows gradual worldly existence on every member of humankind. In that divine aspect, no individual is absent from another; nor are they absent from their Lord; nor is He absent from them. After all, how could the act be absent from its actor? How could something manufactured be absent from its manufacturer?2 This is what God calls malakūt (God’s kingdom, angelic world) in the verse: Thus did We show Abraham the kingdom (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth, that he might be of those who possess certitude

(6:75). He also refers to the same concept where He says: No indeed! Were you to know with knowledge of certainty, you would surely see hell. Again, you will surely see it with the eye of certainty (102:5-7).

What we observe in this world is the worldly aspect of humankind.

That is where individuals are separated from one another, and their conditions and experiences are diversified as they are spread over time and

space, and become subject to the passing of nights and days. That is where people are veiled from their Lord because of orienting themselves toward worldly objectives and sensual pleasures. This aspect is subsequent to the first aspect, and a result of that. The relation between our divine aspect and our worldly aspect is the relation between “Be!” (kun) and “it is” (yakūnu)
